title: EPA Lead Paint RRP Rule: An Investor's Guide
metaDescription: How the EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting rule affects pre-1978 rehabs: certified firms, lead-safe practices, records, and the impact on scope and schedule.
h1: The EPA Lead Paint RRP Rule: What Investors Renovating Pre-1978 Housing Need to Know
dek: If you renovate, repair or paint a house built before 1978 for pay, the EPA's RRP rule requires an EPA-certified firm, a certified renovator directing the work, lead-safe containment and cleanup, and written records. For investors it changes who you hire, how demolition is staged, and what paperwork you keep.
keyTakeaways: The RRP rule applies to paid renovation, repair and painting work that disturbs painted surfaces in housing and child-occupied facilities built before 1978.
The firm doing the work must be EPA-certified (or certified by a state running its own authorized program), and a certified renovator must direct the job.
Lead-safe work means containment, banned high-dust practices, specialized cleaning and a cleaning verification step before the area is reopened.
Records proving compliance have to be kept, and the pre-renovation education pamphlet must be delivered to owners and occupants before work starts.
Treat RRP as a planning input: it affects demolition sequencing, debris handling, window and door scope, and how you schedule occupied units.

sections.h2: What is the EPA RRP rule, in plain terms?
sections.body:
The Renovation, Repair and Painting rule is a federal regulation under the Toxic Substances Control Act. It governs paid work that disturbs paint in target housing, meaning housing built before 1978, and in child-occupied facilities such as some daycares and preschools. The year matters because residential lead-based paint was banned for consumer use in 1978, so any house built before then may have it somewhere under later coats.

The rule does three things. It requires the company doing the work to be certified. It requires a person trained as a certified renovator to be assigned to each job and to direct the lead-safe practices. And it sets work-practice standards for containing dust, avoiding certain methods, cleaning up and verifying the cleanup.

It is not an abatement rule. Abatement is work designed to permanently eliminate lead hazards and is governed by separate requirements and separate certifications. RRP covers ordinary renovation that happens to disturb lead paint: replacing windows, removing trim, opening walls, sanding, scraping, demolishing a kitchen, cutting in a new doorway.

Some states run their own EPA-authorized RRP programs, and some cities layer their own lead ordinances on top. Where a state is authorized, the certification and enforcement come from the state agency rather than directly from EPA, but the core expectations are similar. Before you start work in a new market, confirm which agency certifies firms there and whether the city has any additional lead rules for rentals.

sections.h2: Which jobs on a rehab trigger the rule?
sections.body:
The trigger is disturbing painted surfaces in pre-1978 housing when the work is done for compensation. On an investor rehab, that is almost always the case because you are paying a contractor.

The federal rule has minor-repair thresholds. Interior work that disturbs no more than six square feet of painted surface per room, and exterior work that disturbs no more than twenty square feet, is generally treated as minor maintenance. Those thresholds do not apply to window replacement, to demolition of painted surfaces, or to work using prohibited practices. In practice, a typical flip or BRRRR scope blows past the thresholds in the first day of demolition.

Work that commonly triggers RRP on investor projects includes:
- Window and exterior door replacement, including removing old sashes and stops
- Kitchen and bath demolition where painted walls, soffits or cabinets come out
- Removing or replacing interior trim, baseboard, casing and wainscot
- Exterior scraping and repainting, especially on wood siding and porches
- Cutting openings in plaster or painted drywall for plumbing, electrical or HVAC runs
- Removing a wall to open a floor plan

There are exemptions. If a certified inspector or risk assessor has determined that the components being disturbed are free of lead-based paint, or a certified renovator has tested them with an EPA-recognized test kit and documented negative results, the work practices may not be required for those components. Owner-occupants working on their own home are also outside the rule, but that exemption does not help an investor using paid labor.

sections.h2: What does a certified firm actually have to do on site?
sections.body:
Lead-safe work practices are about controlling dust from the moment work begins until the area passes cleaning verification.

Before work starts, the firm provides the EPA pamphlet on renovation and lead to the owner, and to the occupants if the unit is lived in, and keeps proof that it was delivered. Then the work area is set up. Interior containment typically means covering floors and furniture with plastic sheeting, closing and sealing HVAC registers and doors, posting warning signs, and keeping non-workers out. Exterior containment typically means ground sheeting extending out from the work area, closing nearby windows and doors, and taking care with wind and runoff.

During the work, certain practices are prohibited: open-flame burning or torching of paint, using a heat gun at very high temperatures, and machine sanding, grinding or planing unless the tool has a shroud with HEPA vacuum attachment. Workers clean up as they go, bag debris in heavy plastic, and keep dust from tracking out of the containment.

After the work, the area is cleaned with HEPA vacuums and wet wiping, then the certified renovator performs cleaning verification. For interior work, that means wiping surfaces and comparing the cloths to a verification card, repeating the cleaning until they pass. Some jobs instead use dust clearance testing by a certified professional, which may be required by HUD rules or local ordinances.

None of this is exotic, but it adds steps that a crew used to open demolition does not naturally take. The certified renovator on the job is the person who makes sure they happen.

sections.h2: What documentation should an investor keep?
sections.body:
The firm that performs the work is required to keep records demonstrating compliance for three years after the job. Those records generally include proof of pamphlet delivery, the certified renovator's name and certification, a description of the work practices used, test kit results if any components were tested, and the cleaning verification results.

As the owner, you should ask for a copy of the compliance record at the end of the job and keep it with the property file. There are practical reasons beyond the regulation itself.

First, if you sell a pre-1978 house, the separate Lead-Based Paint Disclosure Rule requires you to disclose known lead-based paint and hazards and any available records and reports, provide the lead warning statement and pamphlet, and give buyers an opportunity to conduct a lead inspection or risk assessment unless they waive it. Having a clean file makes that disclosure straightforward and keeps you from guessing about what was done.

Second, if you lease the property, the same disclosure rule applies to tenants. Some cities also require lead inspections or certificates for rentals built before 1978, and the compliance record from your rehab is evidence you will want if a tenant or code inspector raises the question later.

Third, lenders, insurers and institutional buyers increasingly ask for renovation documentation during due diligence. A folder containing the RRP record, permits, inspection sign-offs and lien waivers is the kind of package that answers questions before they are asked. Genstone keeps that kind of documentation as part of the project file for the clients it renovates for.

sections.h2: How does RRP change your rehab scope?
sections.body:
The rule does not tell you what to renovate, but it does change the cost and logic of certain decisions, so it belongs in your scope conversation early.

Windows are the clearest example. Original wood windows in older houses are often the largest single source of lead dust because friction surfaces grind paint every time the sash moves. Replacement triggers full RRP practices, but once the old sashes are gone, that hazard source is gone too. On a rental you plan to hold, replacing rather than repainting windows can reduce ongoing lead risk and future maintenance. On a flip, it is also a strong buyer-facing upgrade.

Trim and doors are the next decision. Stripping and refinishing painted original trim is labor-intensive under lead-safe rules because dry scraping must be controlled and power sanding requires HEPA-shrouded tools. Replacing trim may cost less in labor and leaves fewer lead-painted surfaces behind. The trade-off is character, which matters more in some neighborhoods than others.

Exterior paint is another. Wood siding on a pre-1978 house usually needs scraping before repainting, and exterior containment adds setup time. Covering or replacing siding changes the calculation, though covering is not removing, and any future disturbance will still need lead-safe practices.

Finally, think about what you leave behind. Stable, intact lead paint under newer coats is generally not a hazard. Deteriorated paint on friction and impact surfaces, porches, window wells and floors is. A scope that addresses deteriorated paint on those surfaces protects future occupants and reduces the chance of a lead problem showing up after you sell or lease.

sections.h2: How does RRP affect the schedule?
sections.body:
Lead-safe work adds time in predictable places. Knowing where lets you plan around it rather than absorb it as slippage.

Setup and teardown take longer. Every interior containment area has to be built before demolition and taken down only after cleaning verification passes. On a whole-house gut, crews can contain large zones at once. On a phased job or an occupied unit, containment is rebuilt for each phase, which adds setup cycles.

Demolition is slower and more deliberate. Crews mist surfaces to keep dust down, bag debris as they go and avoid shortcuts like dry sweeping. Debris has to be contained on the way to the dumpster, which affects how you plan dumpster placement and access.

Cleaning verification is a gate. The next trades should not come into a work area until it passes. If you schedule drywall or paint crews to arrive the morning after demolition without allowing for cleanup and verification, they will either wait or walk into an area that is not ready.

Occupied units carry the most schedule risk. Residents and their belongings have to be protected, work zones closed off, and the occupied space kept clean at the end of each day. This is a common reason small multifamily rehabs move to vacant-unit phasing when possible.

The practical move is to sequence demolition of painted components early and in larger zones, finish verification before rough-in trades arrive, and build containment time into the plan from day one. A contractor who quotes a pre-1978 job without mentioning any of this has either not thought about it or does not plan to follow it.

sections.h2: What are the risks of ignoring the rule?
sections.body:
Some investors still hire crews that skip lead-safe practices on older houses because it looks cheaper and faster on paper. The risks fall into three groups.

The first is regulatory. EPA and authorized states enforce the rule, and enforcement actions have involved contractors, property managers and landlords. Penalties under federal law can be substantial per violation, and a single job can involve several violations, such as failure to be certified, failure to provide the pamphlet and failure to keep records. Investors who direct the work or knowingly hire uncertified firms do not get a pass simply because they did not hold the scraper.

The second is liability. Lead poisoning in a child is a serious injury, and claims arising from renovation dust or from deteriorated paint left behind can follow an owner long after the rehab is done. Insurance policies vary in how they handle lead claims, and some exclude them, so check your own coverage with your agent.

The third is the exit. Buyers of pre-1978 houses get a disclosure and an opportunity to test. Tenants get a disclosure too. Some cities require lead inspections before a rental can be registered or occupied. A property with visible fresh renovation and no compliance record invites questions you would rather not answer during a sale or a refinance.

Compared to those risks, the cost of using a certified firm and building lead-safe steps into the schedule is modest and predictable. That predictability is the point.

sections.h2: How do you vet a contractor for RRP compliance?
sections.body:
Ask questions that require specific answers.

Ask for the firm's RRP certification and confirm it. EPA maintains a searchable list of certified firms, and authorized states maintain their own. The certification is held by the company, so a subcontractor working under your general contractor needs its own if it is the firm performing the renovation.

Ask who the certified renovator will be on your job and how often that person will be on site. The certified renovator must be physically present for certain tasks, such as posting signs, setting up containment and performing cleaning verification, and must be available by phone otherwise.

Ask how containment and debris handling are priced. A bid for a pre-1978 kitchen gut that has no line for containment, HEPA cleanup or lead-safe disposal is either buried somewhere or missing.

Ask to see a sample compliance record from a previous job with the personal details removed. A firm that does this work regularly will have a standard form.

Ask how they handle surprises: lead paint on a component you thought was newer, or a scope change that expands the disturbed area. The answer should involve stopping, extending containment and documenting, not working around it.

Genstone's network work on older housing stock is coordinated through licensed and insured local contractors, and RRP certification is one of the compliance checks that belongs in that vetting for any pre-1978 property.

faqs.q: Does the RRP rule apply if the house is vacant during the rehab?
faqs.a: Yes. The rule applies to target housing built before 1978 regardless of whether anyone is living there during the work, because the concern is both worker exposure and the dust left behind for future occupants. Vacancy makes compliance easier because you can contain larger areas and do not need to protect residents' belongings, but the certification, work practices, cleaning verification and recordkeeping requirements still apply when the work is done for pay.

faqs.q: Can I just test the paint and skip lead-safe practices if it comes back negative?
faqs.a: You can avoid the work practices for specific components that are properly shown to be free of lead-based paint. That determination must come from a certified inspector or risk assessor, or from a certified renovator using an EPA-recognized test kit on each component to be disturbed, and the results must be documented. Testing one wall does not clear the whole house. On a heavily layered older home, testing every component often costs more effort than simply treating the job as lead-safe from the start.

faqs.q: Does the rule apply to houses built in 1978 or later?
faqs.a: No. The federal RRP rule applies to target housing, which is housing constructed before 1978, along with child-occupied facilities built before then. Houses built in 1978 or later are outside the rule. Be careful with construction dates, though. Public records sometimes show the date of a major remodel or are simply wrong, so check permit history and the house itself if a date looks borderline. Some local lead ordinances may also use different criteria.

faqs.q: Is RRP the same as lead abatement?
faqs.a: No. Abatement is work designed specifically to permanently eliminate lead-based paint hazards, such as enclosure, encapsulation or full removal, and it requires different certifications for workers and supervisors. RRP covers ordinary renovation that disturbs lead paint as a side effect. Some government programs, rental registration ordinances or HUD-assisted projects may require hazard reduction or abatement-level work, so confirm what your financing and local rules require before setting scope.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for RRP compliance, the owner or the contractor?
faqs.a: The certified firm performing the work carries the primary compliance obligations: certification, assigning a certified renovator, following work practices and keeping records. That does not make the owner irrelevant. If you, a property manager or a landlord direct paid renovation work in pre-1978 housing, regulators may look at your role as well, and you carry the disclosure obligations when you sell or lease. The simplest protection is hiring a certified firm and keeping its compliance record in your property file.
